description: Routes, middleware, databases, secrets — the server side.

screens.body: A server is a program that listens for requests and sends responses. Frameworks like Express (Node) give you routing: 'when a GET hits /api/tasks, run this function.' That function is a route handler.
screens.heading: What a server does

screens.body: Routing maps URLs to code. /api/tasks → list tasks. /api/tasks/123 → one task. The :id part is a route parameter — the server reads it to know WHICH task you mean.
screens.heading: Routing

screens.body: Middleware runs between the request arriving and your handler — perfect for cross-cutting stuff: check the auth token, log the request, parse JSON bodies. If auth fails, the middleware stops the request before it reaches your code.
screens.heading: Middleware

screens.body: The server talks to the database — never the client. The handler queries the DB (get tasks, save a task), then sends the result back as JSON. With Supabase, your 'server' is partly managed for you — but the rule stands.
screens.heading: Talking to the database

screens.body: API keys, database passwords, secrets — they live in environment variables (a .env file), never in your code. Your code reads process.env.DB_PASSWORD. The .env file is gitignored so secrets never hit GitHub. Remember your Byte setup? Same idea.
screens.heading: Environment variables

screens.body: Three rules: 1) Never trust the client — validate everything on the server. 2) Never build SQL by gluing strings together (SQL injection) — use parameterized queries. 3) Hash passwords; never store or compare plain text.

options: Validate input, parameterize queries, hash passwords

screens.heading: Security basics

screens.body: Supabase is backend-as-a-service: database + auth + API in one. Row Level Security (RLS) is how you say 'users can only read their own tasks' — it's the security layer. That warning email you got? That's RLS doing its job of telling you a table was wide open.
